The Yellowtail rockfish Sebastes flavidus is a long-lived viviparous species inhabiting the continental shelf of the northeastern Pacific. Maximum reported total length in this species reaches 66 cm [Li = 66 cm], a size achieved only after decades of slow, sustained growth typical of many rockfishes. In contrast, the total length at which 50% of individuals are estimated to have attained sexual maturity has been placed at approximately 36 cm [Lp = approximately 36 cm], a threshold that corresponds to a substantial fraction of the ultimate length. Field surveys off the coast of Oregon have consistently recorded mature females exceeding this length, confirming the size-based onset of reproductive capability. The transition from immature to mature size classes is marked by a pronounced shift in energy investment, with somatic growth slowing as resources are increasingly directed toward vitellogenesis and gestation. This pattern of delayed maturity relative to maximum size is a common life-history strategy among iteroparous Sebastes species, serving to buffer against environmental stochasticity by extending the reproductive window.

Reproductive output in S. flavidus is closely tied to female body size, and the wet weight at puberty provides a useful physiological reference point. At the length of 36 cm at puberty, the corresponding body mass calculated from length-weight relationships is approximately 644 grams [Wwp = approximately 644 grams]. This value represents the mass at which females are first capable of contributing to the next generation, and it stands in marked contrast to the ultimate wet weight of 4,200 grams [Wwi = 4,200 grams] attained by large adults. The more than sixfold increase in body mass from puberty to the asymptotic size underscores the substantial scope for post-maturity growth characteristic of this species. Such a trajectory allows females to increase fecundity incrementally with each successive spawning season, as larger body cavities can accommodate larger broods. The length-weight conversion used to derive these mass estimates follows a power function with a slope typical of fusiform marine teleosts, and the values align closely with those reported for other commercially important rockfish species in the genus.

At the opposite end of the size spectrum, the initial offspring mass is remarkably small. Given the viviparous mode of reproduction in S. flavidus, developing embryos are retained internally and nourished via a yolk sac until parturition. The estimated wet weight of a newly released larva, derived from a mean egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters prior to fertilization, is approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams]. This minuscule birth mass reflects the extreme numerical fecundity strategy common among oviparous and viviparous marine fishes, where a huge number of tiny offspring are produced to offset high larval mortality. The larval stage is pelagic and planktonic, with the free-swimming larva relying on its endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The transition to the exotrophic larval phase is a critical bottleneck, and survival during this period is strongly modulated by water temperature and prey availability in the mixed layer.

Under the thermal conditions prevailing in the species' central California nursery grounds, where the temperature is typically around 5.9 °C [T = 5.9 °C], the maximum reproductive rate has been characterized through a combination of fecundity and spawning frequency estimates. Gravid females extrude a single brood of partially developed larvae per year [F_R_i = single brood of partially developed larvae per year], with the total number of larvae per brood scaling with female mass. The annual brood size for a large, mature female can reach approximately 5,500 larvae per brood [N_R_i = approximately 5,500 larvae per brood]. These values combine to yield a substantial yearly reproductive output for an individual that has attained asymptotic size. The reproductive cycle is tightly synchronized with seasonal upwelling events, which enhance planktonic productivity and improve the likelihood of successful larval feeding. This single, synchronized annual spawning event is a common feature among temperate Sebastes species and contrasts with the multiple-batch spawning observed in some tropical congeners.

Longevity in S. flavidus is exceptionally high among marine teleosts, with the maximum documented lifespan reaching 23,360 days [am = 23,360 days] when held at the water temperatures typical of its depth range, approximately 5.9 °C [T = 5.9 °C]. Such extended lifespans are thought to be a consequence of low natural adult mortality and a slow metabolic rate linked to cold-water residence. The physiological trade-off for this longevity is a delayed onset of reproduction, as females do not contribute larvae until they have reached the aforementioned size and mass thresholds. The combination of extreme longevity, substantial asymptotic mass, and low annual fecundity relative to body size defines a classic bet-hedging life-history strategy. Population viability analyses rely heavily on these demographic parameters to evaluate the resilience of S. flavidus stocks to commercial fishing pressure and climate-induced shifts in ocean temperature.
